endorsements.quote: Third, treat the deployed model as a regulated instrument under continuous quality control, not a validated-once oracle.

Hematology’s classifications move fast, as World Health Organization (WHO), International Consensus Classification (ICC), and European LeukemiaNet (ELN) criteria are revised on timescales of months [17], so a model correct today decays tomorrow; dataset shift is a recognized cause of clinical AI failure and demands monitoring, versioned knowledge corpora, and scheduled revalidation [18].
Responsible deployment grants the most independence on structured tasks and forces deference or abstention on the rest.

An agent that ingests free-text notes processes identifiable patient data at scale, so data minimization, local deployment, audit logging, and explicit patient consent for AI-assisted decisions are prerequisites, not afterthoughts [24].
Interface design, abstention behavior, and the physician’s redefined role are part of the intervention, not cosmetic add-ons.

The defensible near-term use is agentic support on structured, auditable tasks: documentation and data extraction [12], guideline-anchored triage and case structuring [1], and variant and risk-classification triage [26], each with mandatory abstention on rare or ambiguous cases and full traceability.

unlisted_practices: Validate agentic AI by evaluating the chain of actions (trajectories) rather than only final answers, using prospective, silent, real-workflow testing.
Allocate AI autonomy inversely to case complexity, granting most independence on structured guideline-defined tasks and requiring deference or abstention on rare or ambiguous cases.
Build calibrated uncertainty and abstention ("I don't know") behavior into clinical AI systems as a core safety feature.
Do not deploy fully autonomous AI for therapeutic decision-making.
Clinicians should not defer to authoritative-sounding AI outputs or treat benchmark performance as a warranty.

Regulators and professional bodies should set rules for AI-assisted harm liability, credentialing analogous to device approval, post-deployment surveillance, and reimbursement tied to monitored performance.
Validate AI models across diverse care settings, including community settings, rather than only a few academic centers.
Use outcome-anchored validation rather than relying solely on concordance with tumor-board decisions as the reference standard.
